content: The conifers, classified under the division Pinophyta (also known as Coniferae), represent one of the 13 or 14 division-level taxa within the plant kingdom (Plantae). These plants are seed-bearing and produce cones, with vascular tissue present in all members. All living conifers are woody plants, predominantly trees, though a few species exist as shrubs. Examples of conifers include cedars, Douglas-firs, cypresses, firs, junipers, kauris, larches, pines, redwoods, spruces, and yews. Conifers are found naturally across nearly all parts of the world and often dominate their habitats, such as in the taiga biome. Economically, conifers are highly valuable, primarily for timber and paper production, with their wood commonly referred to as softwood. The division contains approximately 630 living species. The earliest conifers date back to the late Carboniferous period (Pennsylvanian epoch). The naming of higher plant taxa (above the family rank) is typically derived from the name of an included family, such as Pinaceae (the pine family), or is descriptive. For conifers, the name Coniferae is widely used, though older scientific names like Coniferophyta and Coniferales are no longer valid. According to the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN), names can be formed by replacing the -aceae suffix in a family name (e.g., Pinaceae) with the appropriate termination for the division, such as -ophyta (e.g., Pinophyta). Alternatively, descriptive botanical names may also be used at ranks above the family level. Conifers are often equated with gymnosperms, particularly in temperate climates where they are the most common gymnosperms. However, gymnosperms encompass four distinct groups, with conifers being the largest and most economically significant. The division Pinophyta consists of a single class, Pinopsida, which includes both living and fossil taxa. Historically, living conifers were sometimes divided into two orders: Taxales (containing only Taxaceae) and Pinales (the rest). However, recent DNA research has shown that excluding Taxales from Pinales renders the latter paraphyletic, and Taxales is no longer considered a distinct order. A more accurate subdivision would involve splitting the class into three orders: Pinales (containing only Pinaceae), Araucariales (containing Araucariaceae and Podocarpaceae), and Cupressales (containing the remaining families, including Taxaceae). However, this division has not gained significant support, and most experts prefer to retain all families within a single order, Pinales, despite their ancient origins and diverse morphology. Conifers are now recognized as comprising six to eight families, with 65–70 genera and approximately 600–630 species (696 accepted names). Some interpretations suggest that Cephalotaxaceae may be better included within Taxaceae, and some authors recognize Phyllocladaceae as distinct from Podocarpaceae. The family Taxodiaceae is now included within Cupressaceae but was widely recognized in the past and is still mentioned in many field guides. Conifers are an ancient group, with a fossil record extending back about 300 million years to the late Carboniferous period. Many modern genera are recognizable from fossils dating back 60–120 million years. Other extinct classes and orders of conifer-like plants also appear in the fossil record, particularly from the late Paleozoic and Mesozoic eras. Fossil conifers included diverse forms, some of which were herbaceous and lacked woody stems. Major fossil orders of conifers or conifer-like plants include Cordaitales, Vojnovskyales, Voltziales, and possibly Czekanowskiales (which may be more closely related to Ginkgophyta). All living conifers are woody plants, with most being trees that exhibit monopodial growth (a single, straight trunk with side branches) and strong apical dominance. Mature conifers vary in size, ranging from less than one meter to over 100 meters in height. The tallest, largest, thickest, and oldest living organisms on Earth are all conifers. For example, the Great Basin Bristlecone Pine (Pinus longaeva) is the oldest known living tree, at 4,700 years old. The leaves of many conifers are long, thin, and needle-like, while others, such as most Cupressaceae and some Podocarpaceae, have flat, triangular, scale-like leaves. Some genera, like Agathis (Araucariaceae) and Nageia (Podocarpaceae), have broad, flat, strap-shaped leaves. In most conifers, leaves are arranged spirally, except in most Cupressaceae and one genus in Podocarpaceae, where they are arranged in opposite pairs or whorls. The stomata on conifer leaves are arranged in lines or patches and can close during dry or cold conditions. The leaves are often dark green, which may help absorb maximum energy from weak sunlight in high latitudes or under forest canopy shade. Some species, like the Blue Spruce (Picea pungens), have a strong glaucous wax coating to reflect ultraviolet light. Most conifers are evergreen, retaining their leaves for several years before shedding them. However, five genera (Larix, Pseudolarix, Glyptostrobus, Metasequoia, and Taxodium) are deciduous, shedding their leaves in autumn and remaining leafless through winter. Seedlings of many conifers, including most Cupressaceae and Pinus in Pinaceae, exhibit a distinct juvenile foliage period with leaves that differ markedly from the typical adult leaves. Conifers reproduce via cones. Most are monoecious, though some are subdioecious or dioecious, and all are wind-pollinated. Conifer seeds develop inside protective cones called strobili. The cones take 4 months to 3 years to mature and vary in size from 2 mm to 600 mm. In families like Pinaceae, Araucariaceae, Sciadopityaceae, and most Cupressaceae, the cones are woody, and the scales open when mature to release seeds, which are dispersed by wind. In some species, such as pines that produce edible pine nuts, seeds are dispersed by birds like nutcrackers and jays, which break apart specially adapted softer cones. In fire-adapted pines, seeds may remain stored in closed cones for up to 60–80 years, being released only when a fire kills the parent tree. In families like Podocarpaceae, Cephalotaxaceae, Taxaceae, and one Cupressaceae genus (Juniperus), the cone scales are soft, fleshy, sweet, and brightly colored, attracting fruit-eating birds that disperse the seeds in their droppings. These fleshy scales are known as arils (except in Juniperus). In some species, such as those in Cephalotaxaceae, several cone scales develop into individual arils, resembling a cluster of berries. Male cones produce yellowish pollen in structures called microsporangia. Pollen is carried by the wind to female cones, where it fertilizes the female gametophyte, resulting in a zygote that develops into an embryo. The embryo, along with its surrounding integument, becomes a seed, which may eventually fall to the ground and grow into a new plant. Conifers are ecologically significant, dominating vast areas of land, particularly in boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere and cool mountain climates further south. Many conifers produce distinctively scented resin, which protects the tree from insect infestations and fungal infections. Fossilized resin hardens into amber. Despite their relatively small number of species, conifers play a crucial role in global ecosystems.
